units.oneLiner: Keep every key in the slot array itself and, when the home slot is taken, probe the next slot and the next: the probes stay inside the cache line the first one fetched, Knuth's 1963 formulas say exactly what each load factor costs, and the price is clustering, which is why the table resizes before it is full and why the hash must scatter neighbors.
units.description: Linear probing on 65,536 slots against Knuth's 1963 formulas (within 1% to load 0.7) and a Python set over 1,200,000 operations: at load 0.9 a hit costs 5.315 probes but 1.540 cache lines against 2.570 and 2.570 for double hashing; clusters of 715 slots; tombstones 5.864 probes per miss against 1.698 for backward shift; a weak hash costs 1,056 probes per hit.
units.time: O(1) expected; (1 + 1/(1 - a)) / 2 probes per hit

units.plan_row: Open addressing × Linear probing. Puzzle 172, data-structures (problemSlug hash-collision-resolution, the atlas problem page carrying "Cache-friendly hashing"; sibling live lesson cuckoo-hashing-two-table-eviction-kicks). Solution open_addressing_linear_probing.py (3.0s, prints OK): linear probing with tombstone or backward-shift deletion and a rebuild at 85% live-plus-tombstones, quadratic probing (triangular offsets), double hashing (odd stride), separate chaining, Robin Hood, Fibonacci and weak hashes, a probe-and-cache-line counter (8 slots per 64-byte line, one line per chaining node). ORACLES: (1) Knuth 1963 at loads 0.25 / 0.5 / 0.7 / 0.8 / 0.9 / 0.95: hits 1.164 / 1.509 / 2.172 / 3.027 / 5.962 / 11.609 against 1.167 / 1.500 / 2.167 / 3.000 / 5.500 / 10.500, misses 1.397 / 2.510 / 5.971 / 12.655 / 50.434 / 205.639 against 1.389 / 2.500 / 6.056 / 13.000 / 50.500 / 200.500 (within 6% to 0.8, 20% beyond); (2) 1,200,000 mixed operations across six structures all matching a Python set, final sizes matching; (3) the race at load 0.9 (every key looked up, 5,000 misses): linear probing 5.315 probes/hit, 47.975/miss, 1.540 lines/hit, variance 277, max 612, longest cluster 715; Robin Hood 5.315 / 5.644 / 1.540 / 19.8 / 29; quadratic 2.850 / 12.055 / 1.951 / 16.2 / 92; double hashing 2.570 / 10.056 / 2.570 / 11.1 / 68; chaining 2.450 / 1.923 / 2.450 / 0.5 / 9; longest run by load 8 / 31 / 85 / 209 / 752 / 3,250; (4) deletion: fill to 0.7, delete half: tombstones 5.864 probes per miss (formula for 0.7: 6.056), backward shift 1.698 (formula for 0.35: 1.683); (5) weak hash (high bits) on 2,048 consecutive keys in 4,096 slots: linear probing 1,056 probes per hit, double hashing 8.3, chaining 402.8, strong hash 1.50. Honest: linear probing pays twice double hashing's probes at 0.9 and wins only on lines; the Robin Hood mean is identical to 1e-9 (the displacement total is invariant), asserted; three author notes recorded (quadratic vs double ordering; the first weak-hash experiment at 65,536 slots ran quadratic for ten minutes and was shrunk; a 5,000-key hit sample was replaced by every key after the early-inserted keys biased it). Cards: self, Hash table with chaining, Robin Hood hashing, Cuckoo hashing (live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: linear probing with a hash that keeps neighbors neighbors. Figure: Knuth's hit and miss curves with the measured points beside bars of the longest run by load; cite Knuth 1963 / TAOCP 3 6.4, Amdahl et al. 1954, Pagh-Pagh-Ruzic STOC 2007 DOI 10.1145/1250790.1250839. Viz LinearProbingViz: a 64-slot table as eight cache lines filling to load 0.9, walked slots amber and touched lines outlined, the running average probes per insert against Knuth's expectation, every key checked reachable from its home each tick; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles x 21 ticks, 0 breaks; stepMs 500, holdTicks rests. Preserved narration: Aoede + Algieba.

units.oneLiner: Scan from the right for the longest non-increasing suffix, swap the element before it with the rightmost suffix element larger than it, reverse the suffix: Narayana's fourteenth-century rule visits every arrangement of a multiset exactly once in dictionary order, in place with two indices, at a constant amortized cost per step (mean suffix e - 1), where the single-swap orders of Heap and Johnson-Trotter are cheaper per step and unsorted.
units.description: Algorithm L against itertools for every n to 8 and the multinomial on MISSISSIPPI (34,650): all 362,880 arrangements of nine in 0.12 s with a mean suffix of 1.718 = e − 1 and 1.54 swaps per step; Heap and Johnson-Trotter use 5,039 single swaps but break sorted order 2,513 and 2,519 times; Lehmer unranking matches on 2,000 ranks.
units.time: O(1) amortized per arrangement (mean suffix e − 1); O(n) for one worst step
units.space: O(1) extra: two indices, in place
units.baseline: Heap's algorithm (one swap per arrangement, unsorted)
units.plan_row: Lexicographic permutations × Next-permutation algorithm. Puzzle 206, dp-combinatorics (problemSlug permutation-generation, the atlas problem page carrying "Permutation generation"; sibling live lessons fisher-yates-uniform-swaps (puzzle 46) and held-karp-bitmask-states (puzzle 81)). Solution lexicographic_permutations_next_permutation_algorithm.py (1.6 s, prints OK, 21 checks): Algorithm L with counters for comparisons, swaps, moves, and suffix length; a lexicographic enumerator; Heap's algorithm (iterative); Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter with Even's directions; Lehmer rank and unrank; a copying recursion; next bigger number by rule and by brute force. ORACLES: (1) the rule equals itertools.permutations for n = 1 to 8 (40,320 at n = 8), each arrangement strictly greater than the last; (2) multisets [0,0,1,1,2], [0,0,0,1,1,2,2], MISSISSIPPI (34,650), [1,1,1,1] each listed once, equal to sorted(set(permutations)) and the multinomial; (3) over the full enumeration at n = 8 and 9: mean suffix 1.718 (asserted within 0.01 of e − 1 = 1.718), comparisons 3.077, swaps 1.543 (asserted in 1.50 to 1.60), moves 3.086 per step; n = 9 (362,880) in 0.12 s; (4) Heap's algorithm at n = 7: 5,040 arrangements each once, 5,039 swaps, 2,513 descents, sorted set equal to the lexicographic list; Johnson-Trotter: 5,040 once, 5,039 swaps each of two adjacent positions, 2,519 descents; Algorithm L 0 descents; (5) unrank(k, 8) equals the k-th sequential arrangement and rank inverts it on 2,000 random k plus k = 0, 1, 40,319; (6) 12! = 479,001,600 would take about 3 minutes and 20! = 2,432,902,008,176,640,000 about 26,240 years at the measured n = 9 pace (honest extrapolation); (7) the copying recursion copies 38.7 elements per arrangement at n = 8 and produces the same set; (8) next bigger number with the same digits agrees with brute force on 300 random digit strings of length 4 to 7, 52 with no answer. AUTHOR CORRECTION recorded in the header: the draft guessed 1.36 swaps per step; the measurement is 1.543 because reversing a suffix of length L costs floor(L/2) swaps, mean 0.543 under the 1/k! suffix law; and Heap's one swap per step is cheaper per step but buys no order, which the page states instead. Cards: self, Heap's algorithm, Steinhaus-Johnson-Trotter, Factorial number system × Lehmer code ranking (all algoName pages present). neverUse: regenerating the whole census for one next-arrangement question (40,320 strings for an eight-digit number; 38.7 copies per arrangement). Figure: one step on 1 2 5 4 3 (pivot 2, partner 3, swap, reverse) beside bars of the per-step costs and the descents of the three orders; cite Knuth TAOCP 4A 7.2.1.2 Algorithm L, Narayana Pandita 1356, Sedgewick 1977 (DOI 10.1145/356689.356692). Viz NextPermutationViz: a seeded multiset of five letters, one arrangement per tick with pivot and partner in amber and the reversed suffix in blue, a progress bar against the multinomial count, invariant that each arrangement is greater than the last and uses the same letters and that the final count equals the multinomial; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 28.75 ticks per cycle, 0 breaks; stepMs 170, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Keep one running level and move it a fraction alpha toward each observation: the forecast is the level, and the recursion is a weighted average of the whole past with weights alpha (1 - alpha)^k that fade geometrically, sum to one, and sit (1 - alpha)/alpha values back on average; fit alpha by squared one-step error and it lands on the Kalman gain.
units.description: Exponential smoothing: the recursion equals the unrolled geometric sum to 3e-14; the fitted alpha 0.390 +- 0.003 lands on the Kalman gain 0.390 over 150 series; one-step RMSE 1.284 against a floor of 1.281, moving average 1.321, naive 1.499, mean 4.662; a trend lags by b/alpha (0.96); a season trails by a month, 7.86 against 2.84.
units.plan_row: Exponential smoothing × Geometric decay weights. Puzzle 207, ml-ai (problemSlug time-series-forecasting, the atlas problem page carrying "Short-term forecasting"; sibling live lessons holt-winters-triple-seasonal-smoothing, puzzle 164, and kalman-covariance-correction, puzzle 97). Solution exponential_smoothing_geometric_decay_weights.py (1.2 s, prints OK): the smoothing recursion, the unrolled geometric sum, a coarse-grid plus golden-section fitter on one-step squared error, a local level simulator, the ARIMA(0,1,1) recursion, Holt's linear trend with a grid fit, a moving average, and a compact additive Holt-Winters. ORACLES: (1) recursion = unrolled sum to 2.8e-14 on random series at alpha 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.8; weights at alpha 0.3 sum to 1.000000000000 with mean lag 2.3333 = (1 - a)/a, half the weight inside the last 2 values; (2) local level model q = 0.25: Kalman gain 0.3904, squared-error fit over 150 series of 400: 0.3899 +- 0.0035; ARIMA(0,1,1) with theta -0.6096 forecasts equal to 2.8e-14; (3) one-step RMSE, fitted on the first half and scored on the second half of 150 series: smoothing 1.284 +- 0.005 (MAE 1.026), innovation floor 1.281, moving average 1.321 +- 0.007 (MAE 1.057, best window 4.2 on average), naive 1.499 +- 0.007 (MAE 1.199), mean 4.662 +- 0.176, alpha 0.01: 3.498 +- 0.103; (4) trend b = 0.5 with noise 2 over 60 series: fitted alpha 0.52, one-step lag 0.960 +- 0.008 against b/alpha 0.959, RMSE 2.523; Holt bias -0.001 +- 0.005, RMSE 2.246; (5) h-step intervals over 400 series at the Kalman gain with sigma estimated in-sample: coverage 0.925 (h=1), 0.945 (h=2), 0.935 (h=5), 0.935 (h=10); error variance ratio at h=10 2.35 against 1 + 9 alpha^2 = 2.37; (6) seasonal wave (amplitude 20, noise 2, 40 series): smoothing 7.86 trailing the signal by 1.0 months, seasonal naive 2.84, Holt-Winters (alpha 0.2, gamma 0.3) 2.29. Two author corrections recorded (the trend lag is b/alpha, not b(1 - alpha)/alpha; measured coverage 0.925 to 0.945, not 0.95, so the assertion is a 0.92 to 0.98 band). Cards: self, Moving average × Sliding window, Holt linear trend × Level plus trend smoothing, ARIMA × Box-Jenkins identification (all algoName pages present). neverUse: simple smoothing on a seasonal series (7.86 against 2.84 and 2.29, trailing by a month). Figure: the geometric weights for alpha 0.3 and 0.1 beside log-scale one-step RMSE bars for six methods; cite Brown 1956, Holt 1957 / 2004 (DOI 10.1016/j.ijforecast.2003.09.015), Hyndman, Koehler, Ord, Snyder 2008. Viz ExponentialSmoothingViz: a seeded local level series, one value per tick, the level at the Kalman gain of the drawn q, the geometric weights drawn under the cursor, running one-step RMSE for smoothing, a four-value moving average, and the naive forecast; invariant: the recursive level equals the unrolled sum to 1e-9; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 119 ticks each, 0 breaks; stepMs 110, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Train on what is labeled, score the pool, and buy the label of the one point whose top class the model is least sure of, the point nearest its boundary: three labels saved in four on a four-dimensional boundary, one scoring pass per round, and a blind spot the size of everything the model is confidently wrong about.
units.description: Pool-based active learning with a Newton-trained logistic regression against random sampling, 30 seeds: 13 labels against 44 to reach 0.903 in four dimensions (AULC 0.9072 vs 0.8759, 4.1 standard errors), 2.7 in the plane, none with a wide gap; a hidden cluster got 0 of 40 queries and 0.000 accuracy where random reached 0.838.
units.time: O(|pool| x d) scoring plus one model fit per query
units.space: O(|pool| x d) for the pool and the model
units.baseline: Random sampling from the same pool
units.plan_row: Uncertainty sampling × Least-confidence query. Puzzle 208, ml-ai (problemSlug active-learning, the atlas problem page carrying "Active learning"; sibling live lessons perceptron-mistake-driven-updates, puzzle 130, and thompson-sampling-posterior-draws, puzzle 109). Solution uncertainty_sampling_least_confidence_query.py (7.0 s, prints OK): a Newton-trained L2 logistic regression with a small Gaussian elimination, a pool-based active learning loop taking a strategy, a seed set, and an optional density weight, a softmax regression for three classes, a farthest-first traversal for diversity seeds, and a Gaussian kernel density over the pool. ORACLES: (1) learning curves, 30 seeds, 300-point pool, 400-point test, 2 seed labels, 40 queries, target = Bayes accuracy minus 0.03: four dimensions at separation 3.0 (Bayes 0.9332) least confidence reaches 0.903 in 13 labels against 44 for random, AULC 0.9072 +- 0.0034 against 0.8759 +- 0.0068 (4.1 standard errors of the difference), acc at 10/20/42 labels 0.8991/0.9165/0.9265 against 0.8665/0.8742/0.9036; the plane at separation 3.0: 8 against 8 labels, AULC 0.9180 +- 0.0024 against 0.9063 +- 0.0036 (2.7 SE), acc at 20 0.9223 against 0.9034; four dimensions at separation 5.0 (Bayes 0.9938): 4 against 4 labels, AULC 0.9876 against 0.9883 (-0.4 SE); pool points scored 1,002,600 against 0, 41 model fits per run each; (2) least confidence, margin, and entropy chose the same point on 40 of 40 two-class rounds and disagreed on 21 of 100 three-class softmax rounds; (3) hidden cluster (20 of 260 pool points, class 1 at (-5, 6), seeds from the main clusters), 40 labels, 20 seeds: least confidence 0.00 queries in it, accuracy on it 0.000, main clusters 0.993; random 2.60 queries, 0.838 +- 0.048, main 0.958; farthest-first seed of six then least confidence 8.30 queries, 0.891 +- 0.042, main 0.961, and every farthest-first seed of six lands at least one point in the hidden cluster; (4) 30 random-label noise points scattered among 240 cluster points, 30 queries, 20 seeds: noise among the first 15 queries 0.70 plain, 0.00 density weighted, 2.10 random; AULC 0.8654 +- 0.0057, 0.8610 +- 0.0067, 0.8175 +- 0.0146; (5) cold start at 20 labels: 1 seed per class then 18 queries 0.8808 +- 0.0036, 5 per class then 10 queries 0.8782 +- 0.0038. Three AUTHOR CORRECTIONS recorded in the file: the plane at separation 2.5 showed no gain beyond noise (page uses 3.0 and four dimensions and says the gain grows with the parameters to pin down); density weighting does not fix the hidden cluster (itself sparse), the diversity seed does; the expected outlier chase did not happen with a linear model, so density weighting is reported as removing the few noise queries at no measurable cost. Cards: self, Query by committee × Vote-disagreement query, Diversity sampling × Cluster-representative query, Expected error reduction (all algoName, pages present). neverUse: least confidence on a pool with a region the seed model is confidently wrong about (0 of 40 queries, 0.000). Figure: the hidden-cluster pool with the least-confidence and diversity-seeded boundaries beside the four-dimensional learning curves; cite Lewis and Gale 1994 (DOI 10.1145/188490.188495), Settles 2009 (UW TR 1648), Settles and Craven 2008. Viz ActiveLearningViz: a seeded two-class pool, least confidence against random on the same pool, seeds, and test set, one label per tick for 30 ticks, the next query ringed amber, the boundary blue, learning curves on the right; invariant on every tick: the query is the pool argmax by an independent margin scan, one label per round, probabilities and accuracy finite inside [0, 1]; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Sort the jobs longest first and hand each to the machine that is least loaded so far: the long jobs settle while the machines are empty and the short ones level the ends, so the makespan is never worse than 4/3 - 1/(3m) times the optimum (Graham 1969, tight), against 2 - 1/m for the same rule in arrival order; one sort, one pass, and a lower bound as the receipt.
units.description: Graham's LPT rule against exact optima on 300 random instances: 1.0212 × OPT mean, 1.1739 worst, inside 4/3 − 1/(3m); arrival order 1.1221 and 1.4688; the tight families hit 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 and 2 − 1/m exactly; MULTIFIT wins 148, ties 100, loses 52; LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20 thousand-job instances.
units.time: O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n log m) placements
units.space: O(m) machine loads plus the sorted order
units.plan_row: Job scheduling approximation × Longest processing time. Puzzle 209, optimization-or (problemSlug shop-scheduling, the atlas problem page carrying "Makespan approximation"; sibling live lessons first-fit-decreasing-descending-size-order (131), branchbound-fractional (5), work-stealing-random-victims (114)). Solution job_scheduling_approximation_longest_processing_time.py (0.2 s, prints OK): list scheduling to the least loaded machine, the LPT wrapper, the lower bound max(p, ceil(sum/m)), branch and bound on jobs sorted longest first (one machine tried per distinct load, pruned by the remaining work and by min load + next job), brute force over all m^n assignments, first fit decreasing with a capacity search (MULTIFIT), a move-or-swap local search from the LPT schedule, and the two tight-family generators. ORACLES: (1) exact solver equals brute force on 60 instances of 4 to 8 jobs on 2 or 3 machines; (2) 300 random instances (n = 10..14, m = 2..4, sizes 1..50): LPT/OPT mean 1.0212, worst 1.1739, optimal on 75 of 300, worst by machine count 1.0526 / 1.1111 / 1.1739 against the bounds 1.1667 / 1.2222 / 1.2500; arrival order mean 1.1221, worst 1.4688 (bound 2 - 1/m); MULTIFIT mean 1.0099, worst 1.0833, against LPT wins 148, ties 100, losses 52; local search from LPT mean 1.0045, worst 1.0566, never above LPT; exact search 310 nodes mean, lower bound equal to OPT on 240 of 300; (3) tight families: LPT returns 4m - 1 against OPT 3m, 7/6, 11/9, 15/12, 19/15 for m = 2 to 5 (4/3 - 1/(3m) exactly); the arrival-order family (m(m-1) unit jobs then one job of length m) returns 2m - 1 against m, LPT optimal there; (4) 20 instances of n = 1,000 on m = 10 (sizes 1..100): LPT met the lower bound on 20 of 20, MULTIFIT never below it, arrival order 0.87% above on average and 1.11% at most; (5) adversarial order at m = 10: list 19 against OPT 10 (ratio 1.90), LPT 10; (6) exact search at m = 3 with sizes 1..1000: 988 / 4,795 / 54,121 / 27,022 nodes at n = 12 / 16 / 20 / 24 (asserted more than tenfold growth). Two author corrections recorded in the header: the draft expected LPT about 10 percent above the optimum on small random instances (measured 2 percent), and expected MULTIFIT to tie LPT on most instances (it won about half). Cards: self, Graham list scheduling (arrival order, online), First fit decreasing as MULTIFIT's engine (live lesson badge), Branch and bound (live lesson badge). neverUse: arrival-order list scheduling when the long jobs may come last (19 against 10 on ten machines). Figure: mean and worst ratios for four methods beside Gantt charts of the m = 3 tight family (LPT 11, optimum 9); cite Graham 1966 (DOI 10.1002/j.1538-7305.1966.tb01709.x), Graham 1969 (DOI 10.1137/0117039), Coffman, Garey, Johnson 1978 (DOI 10.1137/0207001), Hochbaum and Shmoys 1987. Viz LptSchedulingViz: a seeded instance of 7 to 9 jobs on three machines placed longest first one job per tick as Gantt bars, the lower bound and the brute-force optimum as dashed marks, the arrival-order makespan in the status line; invariant every placement goes to a least loaded machine and each job is placed once, final check LB <= OPT <= LPT <= (4/3 - 1/9) OPT; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 520, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Stand at each node, check every pair of its neighbors for an edge, and divide the hits by three: the exact triangle count and every local clustering coefficient in one pass priced by the sum of degree choose two, so the hubs decide the bill and the degree-ordered forward algorithm, with every edge pointed uphill, is the escape when they do.
units.description: The node-iterator against four referees: brute force, trace(A^3)/6, and the forward algorithm agree on 40 small graphs and three families (94, 3,615, 205 triangles); ER mean 148.5 against C(n,3)p^3 = 143.8; six hubs take 43.4% of 23,282 pair checks where forward spends 6,550 steps (3.6x fewer); all 35,820,200 triples cost 1,539x.
units.time: O(sum of C(d, 2)) pair checks, the wedge count; forward O(m sqrt m)
units.space: O(n + m): a neighbor set per node
units.baseline: Forward algorithm (edges pointed uphill in degree)
units.plan_row: Triangle counting × Node-iterator. Puzzle 210, graphs (problemSlug subgraph-counting, the atlas problem page carrying "Clustering coefficient"; live rivals Strassen's algorithm, puzzle 31, and Bron-Kerbosch, puzzle 123). Solution triangle_counting_node_iterator.py (0.8 s, prints OK): the node-iterator (per-node triangle tallies, pair checks counted), the degree-ordered forward algorithm (edges oriented uphill, sorted out-list merges counted, largest out-list reported), brute force over node triples, trace(A^3)/6 with a plain multiply, Watts-Strogatz clustering and transitivity, wedge sampling, and Erdos-Renyi, planted-partition, and Barabasi-Albert generators. ORACLES: (1) node-iterator = forward = brute force on 40 random graphs of 10 to 26 nodes, per-node tallies sum to 3T; trace(A^3)/6 = node-iterator = 170 on ER n = 100 p = 0.1 (1,010,000 multiplications against 4,936 pair checks, 205x); (2) three families: ER n = 400 p = 0.02 (1,609 edges, 94 triangles, 12,899 pair checks, 8,609 forward steps, max out-list 7, transitivity 0.0219, average clustering 0.0200), planted 4 x 60 p_in 0.30 p_out 0.01 (2,330 edges, 3,615 triangles, 44,329 checks, 33,510 steps, max out 17, transitivity 0.2446, clustering 0.2468), BA n = 600 m = 3 (1,794 edges, 205 triangles, 23,282 checks, 6,550 steps, max out 6, transitivity 0.0264, clustering 0.0558); (3) hubs: the top 6 BA nodes (degrees 76 to 49) take 43.4% of the pair checks, forward 3.6x fewer steps; ER gains only 1.50x; (4) planted transitivity 0.2446 against an ER twin of equal density (2,273 edges) at 0.0748, 3.3x (asserted > 2.5x); (5) ER n = 120 p = 0.08 over 30 seeds: mean 148.5 +- 4.2 against C(n,3) p^3 = 143.8, mean transitivity 0.0808 against p (asserted within 3.5 SE and 0.01); (6) wedge sampling 2,000 wedges x 20 runs on the planted graph: rms error 0.0111 against predicted SE 0.0096, first estimate 0.2425 -> 3,583 triangles against 3,615 exact, 2,000 closure checks against 44,329 pair checks (every estimate within 4 SE); (7) negative example: all C(600,3) = 35,820,200 triples on the BA graph, 0.71 s, against 23,282 pair checks in about 1 ms, 1,539x the work, both 205 triangles. Three author corrections recorded: the first forward version oriented edges downhill so the hub's out-list held all its neighbors (23,649 steps against 23,282 checks) and the assertion caught it; forward saves only 1.5x on ER, not a big win everywhere; the hubs take 43%, not the guessed half. Cards: self, Triangle counting x DOULION sparsification (wedge sampling and sparsifiers, algoName Triangle counting), Strassen's algorithm x Seven-product block split (trace of the cube, live badge), Bron-Kerbosch x Tomita pivoting (clique enumeration, live badge); forward described in prose, baseline, and the contest table. neverUse: every node triple or a dense cube on a sparse graph. Figure: grouped bars of pair checks against forward steps per family beside the hub-share bar (43.4% from six hubs); cite Watts and Strogatz 1998, Schank and Wagner 2005, Latapy 2008, Chiba and Nishizeki 1985. Viz TriangleCountingViz: a seeded two-community graph of 20 to 26 nodes, one node per tick, pairs checked and triangles counted at their lowest corner, brute force by smallest node as the per-tick invariant, 3T and transitivity at the end; NODE-VERIFIED 20 cycles, 0 breaks; stepMs 420, holdTicks rests. units.oneLiner: Project y onto the columns of X, but do it through the small ledger (X^T X) b = X^T y: one pass over the rows, a p by p Cholesky, the covariance for free, and 0.41x the flops of QR, at the price of seeing the condition number squared, which is harmless until it is not.
units.description: Least squares by the normal equations against Householder QR and the exact Gauss-Markov formulas: Cholesky equals QR to 1.8e-15 at 108,108 flops against 263,870; over 400 seeds the 95% intervals cover 0.951 and the variances match sigma^2 (X^T X)^-1; kappa(X^T X) = kappa(X)^2 on eight degrees until Cholesky fails at degree 12 where QR errs 6.4e-9.
units.time: O(n p^2) to form X^T X, O(p^3) to factor
units.space: the p x p ledger plus one row
units.baseline: Gradient descent on the same objective
units.plan_row: Ordinary least squares × Normal equations. Puzzle 211, probabilistic (problemSlug regression, the atlas problem page carrying "Linear regression"; sibling live lessons gradient-descent-momentum 20, gaussian-elimination-partial-pivoting 133, conjugate-gradient-jacobi-preconditioner 140, ransac-random-consensus-sampling 145). Solution ordinary_least_squares_normal_equations.py (0.4 s, 22 checks, prints OK): pure Python X^T X / X^T y accumulation with flop counters, Cholesky with a non-positive pivot check, triangular solves, the inverse for standard errors, Householder QR, cyclic Jacobi eigenvalues, Hestenes one-sided Jacobi singular values, ridge, gradient descent, Theil-Sen, Huber IRLS. units.oneLiner: Open the first center anywhere, then k minus one times open the next at the point farthest from every center so far: the farthest remaining point and the k centers are k + 1 points pairwise at least the radius apart, so any k centers must serve two of them from one place and the optimum is at least half the radius; a factor-two guarantee in k passes, the best any polynomial algorithm can promise.
units.description: Gonzalez's farthest-first traversal against exact optima on 230 small instances: 1.285 × OPT mean, 1.922 worst, optimal on 20, with r ≤ min witness distance ≤ 2 OPT on every one; exactly 2.000 on k far-apart copies of {0, 1, 2}; on 1,000 points with k = 10 a radius of 2.806 in 1.0 ms against k-means++ 4.185, Lloyd 3.507, PAM 4.478, random 5.546.
units.time: O(nk) distances: k passes over n points
units.space: O(n) for one distance per point
units.plan_row: Greedy k-center × Farthest-first traversal. Puzzle 212, optimization-or (problemSlug clustering, the atlas problem page carrying "K-center approximation"; sibling live lessons kmeans-plus-plus-seeding (puzzle 18) and greedy-set-cover-max-coverage (puzzle 89)). Solution greedy_k_center_farthest_first_traversal.py (2.7 s, prints OK): the traversal with its radius trace and witness, a brute-force exact k-center solver over subsets, the Hochbaum-Shmoys threshold method (binary search over sorted pairwise distances with a greedy cover within 2r), k-means++ seeding, Lloyd, a swap local search aimed at the max or the sum (PAM), and small, large, clean, and tight instance generators. ORACLES: (1) 230 small instances (150 at n = 12, k = 3; 80 at n = 14, k = 4), 113,080 subset evaluations: traversal ratio 1.285 +- 0.013 mean, 1.922 worst, optimal on 20, with r <= min pairwise distance of the k + 1 witness points <= 2 OPT asserted on every instance; threshold method 1.241 +- 0.013 mean, 1.790 worst; random centers 2.089 +- 0.059 mean, 6.788 worst; (2) tight family (k copies of {0, 1, 2} spaced 100 apart, start at 0): radius exactly 2, OPT exactly 1, ratio 2.000 for k = 1..5; (3) n = 1,000 in ten Gaussian clusters with 10% uniform noise, k = 10: traversal radius 2.806, SSE 2,828.1, 1.0 ms; k-means++ seeding over 10 seeds radius 4.185 (worst 5.382), SSE 1,062.2; k-means++ then Lloyd radius 3.507, SSE 600.4, 12.0 iterations; traversal then Lloyd radius 2.607, SSE 675.5, 14 iterations; swap search on the max from the traversal 2.806 (no improvement, 210 evaluations); PAM swaps on the sum radius 4.478, SSE 581.0, sum 626.7 against 1,592.4; threshold method radius 2.501, SSE 1,285.6; random centers 5.546, 1.98 +- 0.08 times the traversal; (4) ten clean clusters of 60, k = 10: radius 1.667; with one outlier at (60, 60) the outlier is center 2 of 10 and the bulk's nine-center radius is 2.711 (1.63x); (5) exact search at n = 16, k = 3..6: 560 / 1,820 / 4,368 / 8,008 subsets (asserted equal to C(16, k)) in 0.03 s; C(1000, 10) = 2.634e23, about 1.4e10 years at the measured pace. Three author corrections recorded in the header: the draft said Lloyd would raise the max radius from any seeding (from the traversal's seeds it lowered it, 2.806 to 2.607); the draft expected single-center swaps to trim the radius (210 candidates found none); the draft expected the threshold method to tie the traversal (it averaged 1.241 against 1.285). Cards: self, K-means (k-means++ seeding, live lesson badge), K-medoids (PAM swaps), Greedy set cover (the threshold method, live lesson badge) (all algoName). neverUse: arbitrary centers for a worst-case cost (2.089 mean, 6.788 worst, 1.98x on the thousand points), with exhaustive search as the opposite mistake (C(1000, 10) subsets). units.oneLiner: Model a mostly blank users-by-items table as a global mean plus two biases plus the dot product of a short taste vector and a short trait vector, and learn the vectors by visiting the observed ratings one at a time, nudging both sides against the error with shrinkage; the blanks are never read, and on planted rank-3 data the fit lands within 0.08 of the noise floor where the biases alone miss by 0.72.
units.description: Matrix factorization by SGD on planted rank-3 ratings (150 x 100, noise 0.5): held-out RMSE 0.583 against the 0.5 floor, 0.328 against the noiseless truth; biases 1.227, mean 1.264; over 5 seeds MF 0.578 ties ALS 0.577, user k-NN 0.950; rank sweep bottoms at 3; k = 20 unshrunk memorizes to 1.060; cold users 1.119; zero-filled SVD 2.831.
units.time: O(observed ratings x k) per pass; 230,280 updates here
units.space: O((users + items) x k) for the factors and biases
units.plan_row: Matrix factorization × Stochastic gradient descent. units.oneLiner: Flood a breadth-first wave from the source pin, labeling every cell it reaches with its distance, until the wave touches the target; then walk the labels back, D - 1, D - 2, down to zero, and the cells you stepped on are a shortest wire. Every label is exact, so the first touch is optimal and a dead wave is a proof that no path exists; the price is labeling most of the grid.
units.description: Lee's wave router on 277 nets across 60 × 60 grids: every path equals an independent breadth-first distance, A* and Hadlock agree, Soukup is longer on 123; 935 cells labeled per net against 338 A* expansions and 316 Hadlock labels; 150 walled grids judged correctly; short-first order 19.2 of 40 nets, rip-up 21.1; greedy failed 231 of 277.
units.time: O(cells within distance D) per net, O(rows x cols) worst case
units.space: one label per labeled cell (12 bits on a 60 x 60 grid), 2 bits with Akers coding
units.baseline: Soukup's line probe with a wave fallback
units.plan_row: Lee maze routing × Breadth-first wave expansion. Puzzle 214, languages-compilers (problemSlug chip-routing, the atlas problem page carrying "Detailed routing"; sibling live lessons astar-manhattan (1), dijkstra-binary-heap (7)). Solution lee_maze_routing_breadth_first_wave_expansion.py (3.0 s, prints OK): a grid generator with random obstacles and straight walls (sealable gaps), Lee's wave with a straight-preferring retrace, the same wave storing only Akers's two-bit codes (1,1,2,2: codes two steps apart differ, so the retrace asks for code(D-1), code(D-2), ...), an independent breadth-first search as the referee, A* with the Manhattan heuristic, Hadlock's detour numbers as a 0-1 breadth-first search, Soukup's line probe with wave fallback, a greedy straight-line router, and a sequential multi-net router with rip-up, immediate reroute of the victims, and rollback. ORACLES: (1) 277 nets on 60 x 60 grids (22% obstacles, 3 walls, targets at least 30 cells away, mean shortest path 49.2): every Lee path valid cell by cell and equal to the independent BFS distance; A*, Hadlock, and the Akers retrace return the same length on every net; Soukup never shorter, longer on 123 of 277 (3.6% extra on average); Hadlock's length equals Manhattan + 2 x detours; (2) cells touched per net: Lee 935 (26% of the grid, about 492 us), A* 338 expanded and 383 peak labeled (about 305 us), Hadlock 316, Soukup 467; A* kept 41% of Lee's cells; (3) completeness on 150 walled grids (15% obstacles, 5 walls, gaps sealed with probability 0.35): 46 connected pairs routed at the shortest length, 104 disconnected pairs refused after labeling exactly the reachable region (asserted equal to the flood fill); (4) 8 grids x 40 two-pin nets (8% obstacles): short nets first 19.2 of 40, long first 13.2, random 16.1, short first with rip-up and reroute 21.1 at 10.9 rip-ups per grid; asserted short-first >= long-first and rip-up >= short-first; (5) memory: 12 bits per label on 60 x 60 against Akers's 2; (6) negative example: the greedy straight-line router failed on 231 of 277 nets and was 13.2% longer when it finished. Author correction recorded: the first rip-up scheme (victims to the back of the queue) completed fewer nets than plain ordering (16.8 against 18.8 of 40 on the first run); replaced by immediate reroute with rollback. Cards: self, A* search × Manhattan heuristic (live lesson badge), Line-probe routing × Escape-line intersection, Rip-up and reroute × Congestion-driven reordering (all algoName pages exist). neverUse: a greedy straight-line router or any no-backtracking probe on a maze. units.oneLiner: Lay a grid, keep the unknown at the points, and replace every derivative by a centered combination of neighbors: the three-point second difference is exact on cubics and errs like h squared, the centered first difference beats the one-sided one by a whole power of h, and the same stencil in two dimensions is the five-point Laplacian; the explicit heat step is cheap only while dt / h^2 stays at or below one half.
units.description: Centered stencils against closed forms: Poisson order 2.00 at every halving (3.2e-3 at 16 intervals to 1.3e-5 at 256), exact on cubics to 1e-14; derivative orders 1.01, 2.00, 4.00 with a round-off floor of 9.9e-12 at h = 3.8e-6; Jacobi 173, 705, 2,834 sweeps vs CG 7, 19, 44; the explicit heat step decays at r = 0.49 and hits 1.9e10 at 0.51.
units.time: O(n) per tridiagonal solve on a line; O(n^2) unknowns on a square with O(1/h^2) Jacobi sweeps or O(1/h) conjugate gradient iterations
units.space: one value per grid point plus the banded matrix
units.plan_row: Finite difference method × Central difference stencils. Puzzle 216, numerical (problemSlug pde-discretization, the atlas problem page carrying "PDE discretization"; sibling live lessons conjugate-gradient-jacobi-preconditioner, gaussian-elimination-partial-pivoting, dormand-prince-embedded-error, fft-cooley-tukey). Solution finite_difference_method_central_difference_stencils.py (0.8 s, prints OK): a Thomas tridiagonal solver, the 1D Poisson solve with the three-point stencil, forward / central / five-point first-derivative stencils, the five-point Laplacian with Jacobi and conjugate gradient, the explicit heat step (FTCS), the implicit theta scheme (backward Euler, Crank-Nicolson), the exact semi-discrete heat solution, and power iteration on the difference matrix. ORACLES: (1) Poisson u = sin(pi x): max error 3.219e-3 (n = 16), 8.036e-4, 2.008e-4, 5.020e-5, 1.255e-5 (n = 256), observed orders 2.00, 2.00, 2.00, 2.00; quadratic x(1 - x) exact to 8.9e-15 and cubic x^3 - x to 1.5e-14; (2) first derivative of exp at x = 1 for h = 0.1, 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125: forward errors 1.41e-1 to 1.71e-2 (orders 1.02, 1.01, 1.01), central 4.53e-3 to 7.08e-5 (2.00, 2.00, 2.00), five-point 9.07e-6 to 2.21e-9 (4.00, 4.00, 4.00); central round-off floor: best h = 3.8e-6 with error 9.9e-12, at h = 1.5e-8 the error is 6.9e-9 (eps / h = 1.5e-8); (3) 2D Poisson u = exp(x) sin(pi x) sin(pi y) with the five-point stencil, CG to 1e-12: errors 1.892e-2, 4.715e-3, 1.183e-3 at n = 8, 16, 32 (orders 2.00, 1.99), CG iterations 7, 19, 44, Jacobi sweeps to a residual of 1e-6 relative 173, 705, 2,834 (growth 4.08, 4.02 per halving); (4) heat equation h = 1/40, 1,500 FTCS steps with a 1e-12 seed: r = 0.49 max |u| 1.0691e-2 against exact 1.0739e-2 (error 4.9e-5), r = 0.51 max |u| 1.890e10; time orders against the semi-discrete exact solution at T = 0.1: backward Euler errors 8.89e-3, 4.49e-3, 2.26e-3 (orders 0.99, 0.99) at r = 8, 4, 2; Crank-Nicolson 7.46e-5, 1.86e-5, 4.66e-6 (2.00, 2.00); FTCS 4.54e-4, 2.27e-4, 1.13e-4 (1.00, 1.00) at r = 0.4, 0.2, 0.1; at r = 8 backward Euler max 0.3818 and Crank-Nicolson 0.3728 against 0.3729; (5) eigenvalues (2 - 2 cos k pi h) / h^2 hold to 1.3e-13 for every k, power iteration 6388.769 against 6390.135, condition number 648 = 4 / (pi h)^2.
